newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Philippines stock plunge leads drop in Asia markets.
newsitem.headline: Philippines stock plunge leads drop in Asia markets.

text.p: A brutal attack on Philippine stocks left that market nearly five percent lower on Tuesday, and other Asian markets followed the trend downward, although less dramatically.
News that the Philippine Central Bank would limit banks' loan exposure to the real estate sector revived old fears of the potential dangers in those markets.

That, combined with expectations of poor corporate earnings, left the composite index above the the low of the day of 2,691.43 but still down 128.87 points, or 4.54 percent, at 2,708.44 points. The property stock index was off 101.58 points, or 7.31 percent, at 1,287.43.
Some analysts took a broader view of the shakeout in the market.
"This has been a savage sell-down. The bottom line is that we are being de-rated with the rest of the region," said an analyst with one foreign investment bank.

While local factors dominated daily trading in most markets, analysts said a note of caution was injected by the spate of economic figures due out in the United States this week which could set the stage for another rise in interest rates.
The figures include a closely watched barometer of wage inflation, the Employment Cost Index and first quarter Gross Domestic Product.
Also, Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan will address the Interim Committee meeting of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank in Washington later on Tuesday.
Dealers will be scrutinising his remarks for any hints of a shift in monetary policy.
Elsewhere in Asia, Thai stocks were battered amid heavy selling, with the key index ending down 13.89 points, or 2.07 percent, to 658.59 points.

Several major banks cut key interest rates a modest 25 percentage points on Monday. But with the central bank likely to maintain a tight monetary stance, traders said the cuts were too small to stimulate the slowing economy.
In Indonesia, profit-taking ahead of next month's election and jitters over property stocks left the composite index down 9.30 points, or 1.42 percent, at the close at 647.23.
Profit-taking set in on property firm Elang Realty, which the Stock Exchange suspended temporarily after the stock fell more than 30 percent on Tuesday.
News of a 367.2 million ringgit trade surplus in February did little to reverse a negative market sentiment in Malaysia, where stocks were pressured by foreign sell orders.

Stocks closed down 15.35 points, or 1.43 percent, to 1,059.51 points after reaching a session low of 1,056.30. "Where do you hide? People are trying to pick the bottom on the market," said Jonathan Duckett, an institutional dealer at Mohaiyani Securities.
Selling by institutions and foreign funds dampened investor confidence in Singapore, where traders were concerned the government may impose new curbs on the property market.
The Straits Times Index ended off 6.59 points, or 0.33 percent, at 1,990.20, after hitting a new year low of 1,981.92.
The Tokyo stock market was closed for a Japanese holiday.
Hong Kong stocks fell on heavy profit-taking in China-related transactions and caution ahead of the U.S. data. The Hang Seng Index finished off 9.75 points, or 0.08 percent, at 12,600.42.
South Korean shares shed 0.11 of a point to end at 704.05. Traders are marking time until the limit on foreign stockholdings is lifted to 23 percent from 20 percent on May 2.
Taiwan stocks closed 68.32 points, or 0.79 percent, lower at 8,592.44 as the market consolidated after its recent advance.
Australia's All Ordinaries Index was up 17.4 points, or 0.71 percent, at 2,479.1 points.
In India, Bombay stocks ended down 16.77 points at a provisional 3,808.74 as the market waited to see if former finance minister P. Chidambaram's party would join the new government.
